message.reasoning_content:
Interesting: There's a conflict. The permissions.html "Permission Model constraints" says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." But the SECURITY.md says "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." This is a genuine conflict in the version-matched docs. I should state the limitation per instructions; don't silently choose.

Let me also check the CLI docs for --allow-fs-read specifics, wildcards, and permission-audit, and the worker_threads docs regarding execArgv and permissions. Also maybe check the "permission model constraints" - I already have the permissions.html text. Let me check the CLI page for --experimental-permission / --permission and --allow-fs-read / --env-file, and the worker_threads page re: execArgv inheritance.

Also, the argument `--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js` — documented: "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So the literal argument grants read of all of /srv/jobs/ (as if /srv/jobs/*), not just .js files. That's a material misreading.

Also symlinks: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories. When starting applications with the permission model enabled, you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links." So job directories containing relative symlinks => escape.

--env-file: "certain flags such as --env-file or --openssl-config are designed to read files before environment initialization... not subject to the rules of the Permission Model." So the env file is read outside permission checks — that's documented; but is it a vulnerability? The threat model says operator-controlled flags are the operator's responsibility; the permission model does not restrict behavior when the operator intentionally configures it.

Open file descriptors: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an already-open fd grants the job read/write (whatever fd allows) bypassing the permission model — os-level access is inherited. That contradicts the assumption that fd passing is constrained.

Also: the model doesn't restrict node:sqlite file access, child_process etc.

--allow-worker: allows creating worker threads. But the docs say the model doesn't inherit to worker thread — which would mean workers may not be restricted at all? Hmm. Actually, historically, the docs said "The model does not inherit to a worker thread" meaning you must pass permissions to the worker via execArgv... But SECURITY.md says workers inherit. This is a documented conflict. Actually let me check the worker_threads doc for `execArgv`/permission. Let's fetch the worker_threads page and the cli page.

Also check the security policy statement: "trusts the code it is asked to run, including JavaScript, WASM and native code... even if dynamically loaded" — so running customer-uploaded JS means the code is trusted by Node's model; permission model is a seat belt, not a sandbox. Also "Exposing Application-Level APIs to Untrusted Users (CWE-653)" — permitting untrusted users to define custom code that executes with the application's privileges is application-level issue.

Let me fetch the CLI docs and worker_threads docs. Maybe also node:vm? The task says at least two distinct official pages; we have two. Let's fetch one or two more for substance: cli.html (for --allow-fs-read, --env-file, --permission-audit) and worker_threads.html (for execArgv/permissions).
